source.title: When Nations Borrow
source.summary: How sovereign debt works, why countries borrow, and what Islamic jurisprudence says about state-level indebtedness.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: Every nation on earth borrows money. The United States owes over $34 trillion. Japan's debt-to-GDP ratio exceeds 260%. But is sovereign debt fundamentally different from personal debt? Classical Islamic jurists debated whether a caliph could borrow on behalf of the ummah, and under what conditions. Abu Yusuf argued that the state treasury (bayt al-mal) should be managed with the same principles that govern individual finances: no riba, no gharar, no burdening future generations with obligations they didn't consent to. This episode explains how sovereign debt works in the modern system, from treasury bonds to central bank operations, and then examines what the earliest Islamic economists would say about a world where every nation is a debtor.

short_video.title: Abu Yusuf vs. Modern Sovereign Debt
short_video.hook: What would an 8th-century economist say about America's $34 trillion debt?
short_video.voiceover: Abu Yusuf, the 8th-century Islamic economist, believed state treasuries should follow the same rules as individual finances. No interest. No speculation. No burdening future generations with debt they never agreed to. Today, the United States owes over 34 trillion dollars. Japan's debt exceeds 260% of their GDP. Every nation on earth borrows money. Classical Islamic jurists actually debated whether a caliph could even borrow on behalf of the community. The principles they established seem impossible in our modern debt-based world.
